_meta.purpose: Educational reference text per lipoma location.

general.what_is_it: A lipoma is a benign tumour made of mature fat cells. It is the commonest benign soft-tissue tumour in adults.
general.how_common: Roughly 1-2 in 100 people have at least one lipoma (estimates vary); peak detection is between 40 and 60 years.
general.imaging_mri: MRI: signal follows normal fat - bright on T1, intermediate/bright on T2 (fast spin-echo), signal drops on fat-suppressed sequences (STIR / fat-sat); thin or no septa; no enhancing nodule.
general.imaging_ct: CT: homogeneous fat density (about -65 to -125 HU), no enhancement. Fat looks DARK on CT but BRIGHT on T1 MRI.
general.imaging_us: Ultrasound: usually ovoid, iso- to hyper-echoic compared with surrounding fat, compressible, little or no Doppler flow.
general.liposarcoma_warning: A fatty mass that is deep, larger than about 5 cm, growing quickly, painful, has thick septa / nodular non-fatty areas or enhances may be an atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma and needs specialist (sarcoma service) review; MDM2 testing on biopsy separates the two.
general.management: Small, painless, typical lipomas: observation and reassurance. Surgical (marginal) excision if painful, growing, cosmetically bothersome, compressing a structure or when the diagnosis is uncertain. Liposuction is an option for some superficial lipomas. Recurrence is uncommon after complete excision of a superficial lipoma and higher for infiltrating intramuscular lipomas.
general.medicines: No tablet or injection is proven to dissolve an established lipoma. Medicines only treat symptoms or complications (for example simple analgesics / NSAIDs for pain, antibiotics for a post-operative infection, anti-seizure drugs for epilepsy linked to an intracranial lipoma). Injection lipolysis (e.g. deoxycholic acid, phosphatidylcholine) is off-label with limited evidence and can cause local reactions. Weight loss or diet does not reliably shrink lipomas. Any drug choice and dose must come from a doctor.

age_groups.under_3: A fatty mass in an infant or toddler is more likely lipoblastoma / lipoblastomatosis than an ordinary lipoma - paediatric specialist review.
age_groups.3_to_17: Ordinary lipomas are uncommon in children. Think of lipoblastoma, lipomatous overgrowth syndromes (e.g. PIK3CA-related), and midline fatty masses over the spine (spinal dysraphism). Intracranial and filum terminale lipomas are congenital and may be found at any age.
age_groups.18_to_39: Lipomas are less common than later in life; multiple lipomas suggest familial multiple lipomatosis (and rarely syndromes such as MEN1 or Gardner).
age_groups.40_to_59: Peak age for typical benign lipomas.
age_groups.60_plus: A large, deep fatty mass in an older adult has a higher chance of being a liposarcoma - keep a low threshold for MRI and biopsy.

adrenal lipoma.how_common: Pure adrenal lipoma is very rare. The usual fat-containing adrenal lesion is a myelolipoma (fat plus blood-forming tissue), found in a small percentage (single digits) of adrenal incidentalomas.
adrenal lipoma.sex_note: Roughly equal in men and women.
adrenal lipoma.symptoms: Usually none (incidental). Large lesions may cause flank/abdominal pain or bleed.
adrenal lipoma.imaging_note: Macroscopic fat on CT/MRI with a thin capsule; no enhancing soft-tissue nodule.
adrenal lipoma.management: Typical small lesions with clear fat need no treatment or routine follow-up. Hormone tests if the picture is atypical. Surgery (adrenalectomy) for large lesions, pain, bleeding or doubtful diagnosis.
adrenal lipoma.medicines: None for the lesion itself; hormonal work-up and treatment only if a functioning tumour is found.
adrenal lipoma.follow_up: Usually none for a classic fatty lesion; repeat imaging if it is large or atypical.

breast lipoma.how_common: A common benign fatty lesion of the breast; exact frequency varies with the population screened.
breast lipoma.typical_sites: Subcutaneous or within breast tissue, any quadrant.
breast lipoma.symptoms: Soft, painless, movable lump; often found on screening imaging.
breast lipoma.imaging_note: Mammography: fat-density (radiolucent) oval mass with a thin capsule. Ultrasound: ovoid, iso/hyper-echoic, compressible. A classic fatty lesion is usually BI-RADS 2 (benign).
breast lipoma.management: Observation if typical. Excision or biopsy if it grows, is painful, looks atypical or the clinical picture does not match the imaging.
breast lipoma.medicines: None for the lesion; analgesics if there is local pain.
breast lipoma.follow_up: Routine breast screening; short-interval imaging only if features are indeterminate.
red_flags: Palpable mass with solid non-fatty component on imaging

cardiac lipoma.how_common: Lipomas are roughly 10% of benign primary cardiac tumours (myxoma is the commonest). Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum is a different, non-neoplastic fatty thickening.
cardiac lipoma.typical_sites: Epicardial surface, within the myocardium, endocardium (right atrium / left ventricle) or interatrial septum.
cardiac lipoma.symptoms: Often none. Palpitations / arrhythmia, chest pain, breathlessness or obstruction when large or intracavitary.
cardiac lipoma.imaging_note: Cardiac MRI with fat suppression and CT show homogeneous fat without enhancement; echo alone cannot prove fat.
differential: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum
cardiac lipoma.management: Asymptomatic: surveillance by a cardiologist. Surgical resection if obstructing, causing arrhythmia or when malignancy cannot be excluded.
cardiac lipoma.medicines: Only for complications (anti-arrhythmic or anticoagulant drugs) and only as decided by a cardiologist.
cardiac lipoma.follow_up: Periodic echo or cardiac MRI if not removed.

cerebellopontine angle lipoma.how_common: About 9% of intracranial lipomas; well below 1% of cerebellopontine-angle masses.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.typical_sites: Cerebellopontine angle / internal auditory canal, often wrapped around the 7th and 8th cranial nerves.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.symptoms: Hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, facial numbness or twitching; many are incidental.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.imaging_note: MRI: T1 bright, signal lost on fat suppression, no enhancement - this separates it from a vestibular schwannoma (enhances) and from a haemorrhagic or dermoid lesion.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.management: Conservative in most patients. Surgery is risky because the lipoma is intertwined with cranial nerves and vessels; reserved for progressive brainstem compression.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.medicines: Symptomatic only (e.g. short-term vestibular suppressants, treatment of trigeminal-type pain) - by a neurologist / ENT specialist.
cerebellopontine angle lipoma.follow_up: Clinical follow-up with audiometry; repeat MRI if symptoms change.

chest wall lipoma.how_common: Common soft-tissue lipoma site; may be subcutaneous, intramuscular or have an intrathoracic (dumbbell) component.
chest wall lipoma.typical_sites: Back and anterior chest wall, around the scapula, between ribs.
chest wall lipoma.symptoms: Painless soft swelling; deep or large ones can be uncomfortable.
chest wall lipoma.imaging_note: Ultrasound / CT / MRI show fat that follows the subcutaneous fat; a thin capsule.
chest wall lipoma.management: Observation or excision for symptoms, growth or doubt; deep and large lesions need MRI first.
chest wall lipoma.medicines: None for the lesion; analgesics for discomfort.
chest wall lipoma.follow_up: Clinical review; imaging if it grows.
red_flags: Deep to fascia and over 5 cm

choroid plexus lipoma.how_common: Rare; intraventricular lipomas are a small minority of intracranial lipomas (intracranial lipomas overall are about 0.1-0.5% of intracranial tumours).
choroid plexus lipoma.typical_age_text: Any age, usually found incidentally in adults
choroid plexus lipoma.typical_sites: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle (usually the atrium), occasionally third / fourth ventricle.
choroid plexus lipoma.imaging_note: CT: very low (fat) density, unlike the bright calcification that is common in choroid plexus. MRI: T1 bright, dark on fat suppression.
choroid plexus lipoma.medicines: None (anti-seizure medicine only if seizures from another cause).

endobronchial lipoma.how_common: Rare; a small fraction of a percent of lung tumours.
endobronchial lipoma.symptoms: Cough, wheeze, breathlessness, haemoptysis, recurrent pneumonia or lung collapse beyond the blockage.
endobronchial lipoma.imaging_note: CT: smooth fat-density nodule inside a bronchus; bronchoscopy shows a yellow polypoid mass.
endobronchial lipoma.management: Bronchoscopic removal (laser / electrocautery / cryotherapy); surgery (bronchotomy, sleeve resection or lobectomy) if lung is irreversibly damaged or the diagnosis is uncertain.
endobronchial lipoma.medicines: Antibiotics for post-obstructive infection and symptomatic relief only - lipoma itself is removed, not treated with drugs.

esophageal lipoma.how_common: Rare; well under 1% of gastrointestinal lipomas, and a small share of benign oesophageal tumours.
esophageal lipoma.typical_sites: Mostly the upper (cervical) oesophagus, submucosal; may be pedunculated.
esophageal lipoma.symptoms: Difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, occasionally a pedunculated lipoma regurgitated into the mouth.
esophageal lipoma.imaging_note: CT: fat density; endoscopic ultrasound: hyperechoic submucosal lesion.
differential: Giant fibrovascular polyp of the oesophagus (can contain fat)
esophageal lipoma.management: Observation if small and silent; endoscopic or surgical removal if over about 4 cm or symptomatic.
esophageal lipoma.follow_up: Endoscopy follow-up if left in place.

filar lipoma.how_common: A fatty filum terminale is found incidentally in roughly 1-5% of people on lumbar MRI (reported range is wide); most are harmless.
filar lipoma.typical_age_text: Any age; incidental in adults, symptomatic tethered cord mostly in children / young adults
filar lipoma.typical_sites: Filum terminale in the lumbosacral spinal canal.
filar lipoma.symptoms: Usually none. If the cord is tethered: back or leg pain, gait problems, bladder / bowel dysfunction.
filar lipoma.imaging_note: Sagittal / axial T1 MRI: bright thickened filum (over about 2 mm) that drops on fat suppression; check that the conus ends at a normal level (above L2-L3).
filar lipoma.management: No treatment when the conus is normally placed and there are no symptoms. Neurosurgical untethering (filum section) when a tethered-cord syndrome is present.
filar lipoma.medicines: None for the lipoma; pain relief and bladder care only as symptoms require.
filar lipoma.follow_up: Clinical review; repeat MRI if new symptoms appear.
red_flags: Skin dimple or tuft over the sacrum

gastric lipoma.how_common: Under 1% of gastric tumours and about 5% of gastrointestinal lipomas.
gastric lipoma.sex_note: Slight female predominance in some series.
gastric lipoma.symptoms: Often none. Lesions above 2-3 cm may cause bleeding from surface ulcer, pain, nausea, or intermittent outlet obstruction.
gastric lipoma.imaging_note: CT: homogeneous fat density; endoscopy: yellow submucosal bulge with 'cushion' and 'naked fat' signs; EUS: hyperechoic.
gastric lipoma.management: Observe if small and silent. Endoscopic (ESD) or laparoscopic resection if symptomatic, bleeding, obstructing or larger than about 3-4 cm.
gastric lipoma.medicines: Acid suppression or iron replacement may be used for associated ulcer / anaemia, but they do not remove the lipoma.
gastric lipoma.follow_up: Endoscopic review if left in place.

hepatic lipoma.how_common: Very rare. Fat-containing liver masses are more often angiomyolipoma, myelolipoma or focal fatty change.
hepatic lipoma.sex_note: Reported more often in women, but numbers are small.
hepatic lipoma.imaging_note: Homogeneous fat on CT / MRI with signal drop on fat suppression; no enhancing vessels (which would favour angiomyolipoma).
hepatic lipoma.management: Observation when imaging is unequivocal; biopsy if doubt; resection for symptoms or uncertainty.
hepatic lipoma.follow_up: Imaging follow-up if not removed, especially in chronic liver disease.

inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.how_common: Lipoma of the spermatic cord is the commonest benign cord mass and is frequently found during inguinal hernia repair (reported in a large share of operations in some series).
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.typical_sites: Inguinal canal and spermatic cord, sometimes extending into the scrotum.
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.symptoms: Painless groin or scrotal swelling; may accompany or mimic an inguinal hernia.
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.imaging_note: Ultrasound: echogenic, avascular mass along the cord; CT / MRI show fat density / signal. Note that herniated omental fat can look the same.
differential: Liposarcoma of the spermatic cord (rare, often mistaken for lipoma)
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.management: Observation if small and painless; surgical excision with hernia repair when symptomatic, cosmetically bothersome or if imaging is not typical.
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.medicines: Only simple pain relief after surgery.
inguinal canal / peritesticular lipoma.follow_up: Clinical review; MRI if large or growing.

intermuscular lipoma.how_common: Less common than intramuscular lipoma; a small percentage of all lipomas.
intermuscular lipoma.typical_sites: Between muscle groups (fascial planes) - shoulder, arm, thigh, neck, trunk.
intermuscular lipoma.symptoms: Deep painless swelling; may compress nerves or vessels.
intermuscular lipoma.imaging_note: MRI: encapsulated fat-signal mass lying between muscles with thin septa.
intermuscular lipoma.management: Excision if symptomatic, growing or large; large deep fatty tumours should go through a sarcoma team before surgery.
intermuscular lipoma.medicines: None for the lesion; analgesics for discomfort.

intestinal lipoma.how_common: Lipomas are the second commonest benign colon tumour after adenomatous polyps; about 65-75% of GI lipomas are in the colon and 20-25% in the small bowel.
intestinal lipoma.sex_note: Slight female predominance in some series.
intestinal lipoma.symptoms: Often none. Over about 2 cm: abdominal pain, bleeding, bowel habit change; intussusception or obstruction (a lipoma can be the lead point).
intestinal lipoma.imaging_note: CT: smooth ovoid fat-density mass; colonoscopy: yellow submucosal bulge with 'cushion' and 'naked fat' signs.
differential: Other lead points for intussusception (cancer is the commonest in adults)
intestinal lipoma.management: Observe if under about 2 cm and silent. Endoscopic or laparoscopic resection if symptomatic, bleeding, intussusception or when malignancy cannot be excluded.
intestinal lipoma.medicines: None for the lesion; iron or fluids only for complications.
intestinal lipoma.follow_up: Colonoscopic follow-up if left in place.

intracranial osteolipoma.how_common: Rare variant of intracranial lipoma that contains bone or calcification.
intracranial osteolipoma.symptoms: Usually none; seizures or headache are possible.
intracranial osteolipoma.imaging_note: CT: fat plus bone / calcification; MRI: T1-bright fat with signal voids from bone.
intracranial osteolipoma.management: Conservative; surgery is rarely justified because of closely related vessels and nerves.
intracranial osteolipoma.medicines: Anti-seizure drugs only if seizures occur (neurologist's decision).

intramuscular lipoma.typical_sites: Thigh (commonest), shoulder / upper arm, trunk, calf.
intramuscular lipoma.symptoms: Deep painless mass that firms up when the muscle contracts; sometimes aching.
intramuscular lipoma.imaging_note: MRI: fat signal infiltrating between muscle fibres (infiltrating type) or a well-circumscribed fatty mass in muscle.
intramuscular lipoma.management: Observe if small and silent; excision if symptomatic or growing - infiltrating tumours need a wider excision and have a higher recurrence rate (up to about 20% or more in some series). Large (over 5 cm) deep lesions: sarcoma-team review.
intramuscular lipoma.medicines: Simple analgesics / NSAIDs for pain only.
intramuscular lipoma.follow_up: Clinical / MRI follow-up after incomplete excision.

intraosseous lipoma.how_common: Very rare - well under 1% (about 0.1%) of primary bone tumours.
intraosseous lipoma.sex_note: Roughly equal or slight male predominance.
intraosseous lipoma.typical_sites: Calcaneus (commonest), proximal femur (intertrochanteric region / neck), tibia, fibula, ilium.
intraosseous lipoma.symptoms: Often none (incidental). Pain in some, rarely pathological fracture.
intraosseous lipoma.imaging_note: X-ray: well-defined lucent lesion with sclerotic rim, sometimes a central calcified nidus. MRI: fat signal if viable (Milgram stage 1); mixed signal with necrosis / calcification / cyst in later stages.
intraosseous lipoma.management: Observation with imaging if painless. Curettage with or without bone graft for pain or fracture risk; protective fixation in weight-bearing sites such as the proximal femur.
intraosseous lipoma.medicines: Analgesics / NSAIDs for pain; no drug removes the lesion.
intraosseous lipoma.follow_up: Periodic X-ray; recurrence after curettage is uncommon.
red_flags: Pain at rest or night pain

mediastinal lipoma.typical_sites: Anterior / inferior mediastinum, sometimes dumbbell-shaped through the thoracic inlet.
mediastinal lipoma.symptoms: Usually none; cough, breathlessness or chest pain when large.
mediastinal lipoma.imaging_note: CT: homogeneous fat (about -50 to -120 HU), may mould around structures without invading them.
mediastinal lipoma.management: Observe if small, silent and typical; surgical resection (VATS / thoracotomy) if symptomatic, compressive or atypical.
mediastinal lipoma.medicines: None for the lipoma; review steroid exposure if the picture is diffuse lipomatosis.
red_flags: Superior vena cava or airway compression

mesenteric lipoma.how_common: Rare; fatty mesenteric masses are more often mesenteric panniculitis, lipomatosis or liposarcoma.
mesenteric lipoma.symptoms: Often none; abdominal distension, pain, bowel obstruction or volvulus when large.
mesenteric lipoma.imaging_note: CT: fat-density mass displacing bowel, thin or no septa.
mesenteric lipoma.management: Observe when clearly a simple lipoma; surgery for symptoms; any large fatty abdominal mass with septa or nodules should be treated as possible liposarcoma until proven otherwise.
mesenteric lipoma.follow_up: Interval CT / MRI if not removed.

pancreatic lipoma.how_common: Very rare. Focal fatty infiltration of the pancreas is far commoner and can mimic a lipoma.
pancreatic lipoma.symptoms: Usually none; abdominal pain, pancreatitis or jaundice if large or in the head.
pancreatic lipoma.imaging_note: CT: homogeneous fat density; MRI: fat that suppresses; EUS: hyperechoic.
pancreatic lipoma.management: Observation if typical and silent; resection if symptomatic or uncertain.
pancreatic lipoma.medicines: Pancreatic enzyme replacement only if generalised fatty replacement causes insufficiency.

paracaval lipoma.typical_sites: Retroperitoneal fat beside the inferior vena cava.
paracaval lipoma.symptoms: Non-specific abdominal discomfort or none; may displace the IVC.
paracaval lipoma.imaging_note: Fat-density mass next to the IVC; main task is to exclude liposarcoma, the commonest retroperitoneal sarcoma.
paracaval lipoma.management: Because retroperitoneal fatty masses are often liposarcomas, MRI and specialist review (biopsy / MDM2) are advised; complete excision is usual.
paracaval lipoma.follow_up: Surveillance imaging after excision (recurrence is possible).

parosteal lipoma.typical_sites: Along the shaft of long bones - femur, radius, humerus, tibia.
parosteal lipoma.symptoms: Slow painless mass; nerve palsy (e.g. posterior interosseous nerve at the forearm) if it compresses a nerve.
parosteal lipoma.imaging_note: X-ray: lucent fatty mass with reactive bony outgrowth on the adjacent cortex; MRI: fat attached to periosteum.
parosteal lipoma.management: Excision (with the reactive bone) if symptomatic or nerve compression is present.

parotid lipoma.sex_note: More often men in several series.
parotid lipoma.typical_sites: Superficial lobe of the parotid gland.
parotid lipoma.symptoms: Soft, painless, slowly growing cheek swelling; facial nerve function is normal.
parotid lipoma.imaging_note: Ultrasound: ovoid mass with thin hyperechoic striations; CT / MRI show fat.
parotid lipoma.management: Observation or superficial parotidectomy / enucleation if symptomatic, cosmetically bothersome or uncertain, with facial-nerve preservation.

pericallosal lipoma.how_common: The commonest site of intracranial lipoma (about 45% of them). Intracranial lipomas are roughly 0.1-0.5% of intracranial tumours / incidental imaging findings.
pericallosal lipoma.typical_age_text: Congenital - found at any age, many in adults as incidental findings
pericallosal lipoma.typical_sites: Along the corpus callosum (curvilinear thin type or large tubulonodular anterior type).
pericallosal lipoma.symptoms: Often none. Seizures, headache, developmental delay or learning difficulty, usually linked to an associated callosal dysgenesis.
pericallosal lipoma.imaging_note: MRI: T1 bright curved or nodular fat along the callosum, dark on fat suppression. Large tubulonodular lipomas are almost always accompanied by corpus callosum dysgenesis.
pericallosal lipoma.management: No surgery - the lipoma is embedded in the pericallosal arteries and removal brings risk without benefit. Manage epilepsy and any associated brain anomalies.
pericallosal lipoma.medicines: Anti-seizure medicines if epilepsy is present (choice and dose by a neurologist).
pericallosal lipoma.follow_up: Clinical follow-up; repeat imaging only if symptoms change.

pericardial lipoma.symptoms: Often none; chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations if large.
pericardial lipoma.imaging_note: CT / MRI: fat mass in the pericardium, no enhancing nodules; must be told from normal (often abundant) epicardial fat.
pericardial lipoma.management: Observe if silent; surgical resection if compressing the heart or when malignancy is suspected.

pleural lipoma.how_common: Rare; most are subpleural / extrapleural fat masses.
pleural lipoma.typical_sites: Between the parietal pleura and chest wall; sometimes dumbbell-shaped through the chest wall.
pleural lipoma.symptoms: Often none; cough, chest discomfort or breathlessness when large.
pleural lipoma.imaging_note: X-ray: well-defined soft-tissue density with obtuse angles against the chest wall; CT: homogeneous fat. Extrapleural fat hypertrophy (steroids, obesity) is a mimic.
differential: Solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura
pleural lipoma.management: Observe if silent and typical; resection (often VATS) if symptomatic, enlarging or uncertain.

quadrigeminal cistern lipoma.how_common: About 25% of intracranial lipomas (second commonest site after pericallosal).
quadrigeminal cistern lipoma.typical_age_text: Any age; usually an incidental adult finding
quadrigeminal cistern lipoma.typical_sites: Quadrigeminal / ambient / superior cerebellar cisterns behind the midbrain tectum, near the pineal region.
quadrigeminal cistern lipoma.symptoms: Almost always none; rarely hydrocephalus or seizures.
quadrigeminal cistern lipoma.imaging_note: MRI: small T1-bright midline nodule, dark on fat suppression; CT: fat density.

subgaleal lipoma.how_common: A recognised cause of forehead / scalp swelling; many lie under the frontalis muscle or galea.
subgaleal lipoma.symptoms: Soft painless swelling, cosmetic concern, sometimes mild headache.
subgaleal lipoma.imaging_note: Ultrasound: ovoid hyperechoic / isoechoic mass under the scalp; CT / MRI show fat with intact skull.
subgaleal lipoma.management: Observation, or excision (often via a hidden hairline / endoscopic approach) for cosmetic reasons, taking care of the frontal nerve branches.

suprasellar cistern lipoma.how_common: About 14% of intracranial lipomas (suprasellar / interpeduncular / tuber cinereum region).
suprasellar cistern lipoma.typical_age_text: Any age; usually an incidental adult finding
suprasellar cistern lipoma.typical_sites: Suprasellar and interpeduncular cisterns, tuber cinereum region.
suprasellar cistern lipoma.symptoms: Usually none; rarely visual or hormonal disturbance.
suprasellar cistern lipoma.imaging_note: Sagittal T1 MRI: bright nodule in the suprasellar cistern that drops on fat suppression; CT: fat density.
differential: Rathke cleft cyst / pituitary haemorrhage (T1 bright)
suprasellar cistern lipoma.management: Observation; surgery is avoided because of adjacent hypothalamus, optic apparatus and vessels. Endocrine and visual assessment if symptoms.
suprasellar cistern lipoma.medicines: None for the lipoma; hormone replacement only if a pituitary / hypothalamic deficit is documented.
suprasellar cistern lipoma.follow_up: Usually none; review if visual or endocrine symptoms.
